description:
Two-person team from Angeles City, Philippines. NASA's two fire sensors, MODIS and VIIRS, read the same ground and their records disagree. BRASA is a free, open-source web app. It folds 26 years of FIRMS active-fire detections into a burning calendar for any area you draw. We validated on years held out of training. Fire managers, land managers and scientists can use it to ask one narrow question: unusual month, or sensor switch inventing a surge?

Live: theexotech.github.io/brasa
summary:
BRASA (Burning Records Across Satellites, Aligned) is a free, open-source web app that harmonizes NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots from MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) into one consistent monthly record, and turns it into a burning-activity calendar for any area a user draws.

The two sensors cannot be compared directly: VIIRS detects 5–10× more hotspots, so a raw splice invents a +429 % (Argentina) to +896 % (Philippines) surge in fire activity. BRASA removes that artefact by deduplicating detections to ~1 km active-fire cell-days and calibrating VIIRS and Terra to Aqua MODIS with month, day/night and empirical-Bayes cell-level ratios. Tested on held-out years, total bias falls to −1.3 % and +0.6 % (R² 0.98 and 0.97), and every converted month carries a 90 % prediction interval.

Users get a year-by-month calendar from 2000 to today, anomalies against the historical median, fire-season and trend indicators, any month's hotspots on a map, live FIRMS detections, and CSV, PNG and JSON downloads, in English and Spanish. As MODIS retires, BRASA keeps a 26-year fire record comparable, so emergency managers can tell an unusual month from a sensor switch.
details:
Live app

Source code (MIT)

Method & validation

Demo deck (7 slides)

For judges: a 60-second tour

The app keeps its state in the URL, so each claim opens exactly where it lives. No account, no setup.

1. April 2026, 60 km around Angeles City, Pampanga: 102 hotspots against a 2003–2022 median of 38 (2.7×).

2. Córdoba, Argentina, September 2020: that month's hotspots on the map.

3. Raw against harmonized, with the leave-one-year-out table

The problem

MODIS (Terra since 2000, Aqua since 2002) holds the only active-fire record long enough to define "normal", and both satellites are at the end of their missions. VIIRS (S-NPP since 2012, NOAA-20 since 2018) carries the record forward with 375 m pixels, so it detects 5× (Argentina) to 10× (Philippines) more hotspots for the same fires. Join the two records and the past rewrites itself: the raw spliced record says 2013 burned 2.9× more than 2003 in Argentina; the harmonized record shows 2003 burned 1.8× more than 2013. Every trend, anomaly and "worst season on record" built on raw counts inherits that artefact.

What it does

- Pick an area: draw a polygon or rectangle, enter latitude/longitude and a radius, upload a GeoJSON, or use a whole region.

- Read the burning-activity calendar: every month from November 2000 to today in one unit, with annual totals, the baseline median row, the data-source era and uncertainty marks.

- Switch to anomalies against a multi-year median (default 2003–2022, target year excluded), shown on a colour-blind-safe diverging ramp.

- See the answer first: latest month vs median (including month-to-date against the same days in past years), fire season, most active year, Theil–Sen trend with significance, and a plain-language situation summary in English or Spanish.

- Click any month to map its hotspots over NASA GIBS imagery, or pull the last three days live from the FIRMS API.

- Download the hotspot CSV clipped to the area, a monthly CSV with 90 % intervals, the calendar as PNG/SVG, a JSON report, or a shareable link.

How it works

1. Clean: FIRMS vegetation fires only, nominal/high confidence; static heat sources removed.

2. De-pixelate: every detection is snapped to a ~1 km cell, one count per cell × day × day/night × platform. This alone cuts the VIIRS excess from 5.1× to 3.2× in Argentina.

3. Calibrate to Aqua MODIS, the reference-satellite approach INPE uses for Brazil's official series, over the stable 2012–2021 overlap: month × day/night ratios plus empirical-Bayes multipliers per 0.5° cell.

4. Relay and quantify: Terra → Aqua → VIIRS → NOAA-20 hand-offs, automatic per-platform outage detection, and a 90 % prediction interval on every converted month from leave-one-year-out residuals.

A Python pipeline (polars) writes compact static files; a TypeScript, MapLibre and D3 site serves them from GitHub Pages. No server, no login.

Validation

Leave-one-year-out over the overlap: each year is predicted by a model fitted on the other years and checked against what Aqua MODIS actually saw.

- Total bias, raw splice → BRASA: +429 % → −1.3 % (Argentina), +896 % → +0.6 % (Philippines).

- Monthly counts on held-out years: R² 0.98 and 0.97 (raw splice: below 0).

- Against the usual single-ratio fix, typical monthly error drops 31 % (Argentina, VIIRS → MODIS) and 68 % (Terra → Aqua).

- Where we do not win: at single 0.5° cell level a single ratio scores about the same as our model. We report it, and small areas get honestly wider intervals.

Benefits and intended impact

- Removes a sensor artefact that would otherwise read as a false alarm or a false trend.

- Answers the first question in any fire briefing, "is this month normal?", for any area, in seconds.

- Keeps the 26-year record usable after MODIS and S-NPP retire; NOAA-20 is already wired in.

- Quantifies uncertainty instead of hiding it.

- Built for early-warning and emergency-response agencies, land and park managers, and scientists. Argentina (with a Spanish interface) and the Philippines (our home) ship today; any other country is one config line and a pipeline run.

What is new

The standard fix is one global conversion ratio. The ratio is not constant: it differs 3.8× between day and night and up to 3.4× across seasons. BRASA fits it per month, day/night and cell, removes pixel multiplicity before fitting, publishes an interval for every converted month, and turns all of it into a calendar a duty officer can read.

Factors we considered

Honest uncertainty and a stated limitations section; colour-blind-safe ramps, keyboard navigation and a table view; English and Spanish; mobile layout; no account, no key and no server, so it costs nothing to run; reproducibility, with every number regenerated from the open pipeline.

Tools

Python, polars, NumPy, Shapely, PyArrow, pytest; TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, D3, Vitest; GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages.

Team

BRASA Dynamics, two people from Angeles City, Pampanga, Philippines: @theexotech (team owner) and @andreirss, father and son; usernames only, because one of us is under 18. Who did what is written out in docs/METHODOLOGY.md §8.
